brief.head: Paid alike, paid wrong
brief.text: Paying all civil ser­vants in India es­sen­tially the same is “a mad idea”, Ajay Shah said: of­fi­cials in rich re­gions are un­der­paid, those in poor re­gions over­paid. {047-C04}

brief.head: Mosquitoes are local
brief.text: Mosquitoes can be con­trolled, Ajay Shah said, but they change every 100 to 200 kilo­me­tres, so con­trol pro­grammes must be de­signed neigh­bour­hood by neigh­bour­hood. {047-C05}

brief.head: The village problem
brief.text: Cities, some big­ger than coun­tries, have the scale to gov­ern, Ajay Shah said. Villages of about 600 peo­ple do not, and he is “not a ro­man­tic about vil­lage level gov­ern­ment”. {047-C09}

brief.head: Votes without power
brief.text: City res­i­dents vote for mu­nic­i­pal of­fi­cials with lit­tle real power, Amit Varma said, cit­ing Shruti Rajagopalan; those who hold power have their vote banks else­where. {047-C12}

brief.head: Brains for every city
brief.text: Janaagraha counts 63 groups of sim­i­lar cities that could share data and re­search, Ajay Shah said. Every state and city, he ar­gued, needs its own thinkers, re­search and crit­ics. {047-C16}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on pushing power down
lead.head: One country, too many countries

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 47

body: India needs far more local gov­ern­ment than it has, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah ar­gued, in an episode that ran from mos­qui­toes to the Catholic Church.

Varma opened with a thought from his re­search for a con­ver­sa­tion with the econ­o­mist Lant Pritchett. Nation-states grew top-down, need­ing taxes and con­scripts. City gov­ern­ments grew bot­tom-up, out of the need for order and basic ser­vices.

“What we have kind of landed up in India with is es­sen­tially just the larger co­er­cive su­per­struc­ture of the na­tion state with no con­cept of what a truly re­spon­sive gov­ern­ment is,” he said. {047-C01}
## Mind the gaps

Shah said the place to start is het­ero­gene­ity. By CMIE sur­vey data, av­er­age in­come in India’s rich­est re­gion is about five times the poorest’s; for young women own­ing mo­bile phones, the gap is 10 to 15 times.
Varma added fig­ures from Nilakantan RS: life ex­pectancy of 75 in Kerala, 64 in Uttar Pradesh; in­fant mor­tal­ity of seven per thou­sand in Kerala, 48 in Madhya Pradesh.
Then there is sheer size. Uttar Pradesh, by Varma’s own cal­cu­la­tion, is as big as France, Germany, Italy and Spain com­bined, run by one state gov­ern­ment.
“India is that di­verse and that het­ero­ge­neous,” Shah said, and every ques­tion of pol­icy must start there. {047-C02}
## Lowest level first

The rule the hosts reached for is sub­sidiar­ity: every func­tion of gov­ern­ment at the low­est level that can do it, Shah said. Currency be­longs at the top. Mosquito con­trol be­longs in the vil­lage or the city. {047-C06}
India runs the other way. The Constitution’s con­cur­rent list, Shah said, was meant for a wise chief min­is­ter and Jawaharlal Nehru to find a mid­dle road. In the fine print, the Union wins.
Planners reached into the state list too, through cen­trally spon­sored schemes that pay 65 per cent if a state runs, say, ed­u­ca­tion the Union’s way. Shah would scrap them.

Cities, he ar­gued, need a slice of GST, which can be traced to the shop where a sale hap­pens. Of a sin­gle rate of about 10 per cent, he would give roughly three to the Union, two to the state and five to the city.
## The heretic speaks

Varma, who said there were two Ajay Shahs, de­manded that the heretic present him­self. The heretic cel­e­brated mi­gra­tion: un­happy cit­i­zens move, and gov­ern­ments that drive them away lose their tax base.

Shah called the lament for mi­grants who left a vil­lage par­adise for a city slum a lux­ury be­lief. “People choose,” he said. “And life in most urban slums is bet­ter than life in most vil­lages.” {#slums}
Varma’s caveat was that Indian states feel the pres­sure only weakly, since most tax money flows to the cen­tre.

Then Shah turned on his own side. “A chief min­is­ter in India is a lit­tle bit of a dic­ta­tor,” he said, barely checked by leg­is­la­tures or cowed state ju­di­cia­ries. {047-C13} It is, he said, “a choice be­tween bad and bad”.
His way out: about a hun­dred states, many of them cities. West Bengal could be­come two or three, one of them Calcutta.
Both hosts ended on cities. Varma chose Jane Jacobs’s *The Death and Life of Great American Cities*, “an ab­so­lute mas­ter­piece”. Shah chose a book the urban thinker Bimal Patel is still build­ing.
Varma’s sign-off: “Decentralization. Let’s do it.”

second.label: History lesson
second.head: Heaven’s org chart
second.deck: Ajay Shah traces the subsidiarity principle back to the Catholic Church

pic.caption: Main facade of Saint Peter’s Basilica in 2015

body: Economists par­rot the sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple as if it were their own, Ajay Shah said. It is older, and it comes from one of the world’s most suc­cess­ful or­gan­i­sa­tions: the Catholic Church. {047-S06}

From around 380 to about 1950, he said, the Church was an im­por­tant or­gan­i­sa­tion in the world. The Vatican con­trolled armies and took part in in­ter­na­tional treaties, and the Church lived longer than most em­pires.

Empires cen­tralised more, and tended to crash. The Church’s de­sign se­cret was the op­po­site. Churches all over the world had their own au­ton­omy, with the ab­so­lute min­i­mum of cen­tral con­trol. Over that long span, Shah said, the se­cret sauce was sub­sidiar­ity. {#secretsauce}

quote.text: Empires tended to crash partly be­cause em­pires did more cen­tral­iz­ing. And one of the de­sign se­crets of the Catholic Church was de­cen­tral­iza­tion.

third.head: Kerala’s three-step lead

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Kerala’s head start on COVID

body: When COVID came, Kerala had a head start. Malayali stu­dents study­ing in China came home and brought the virus with them, Ajay Shah said, so the state was grap­pling with the first surge be­fore al­most any­body else in India. {047-S03}
Kerala has sig­nif­i­cant ca­pa­bil­i­ties in its health sys­tem. It was soon up and run­ning with quar­an­tines, iso­la­tion and a whole bag of tech­niques for the early stages.

For some time, Shah said, the Union gov­ern­ment tried to do ab­so­lutely noth­ing. Then it an­nounced com­plete lock­downs for the en­tire coun­try. Kerala’s health au­thor­i­ties pushed back: “We know what to do. Don’t tell us what to do. We are prob­a­bly three steps ahead of you.”
Amit Varma added that Kerala’s ex­cel­lent gov­er­nance cul­ture pre­dates in­de­pen­dence, going back decades if not cen­turies. {#predates}

p2.title: Where power belongs
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah, chapter by chapter, on why India must push power downwards, and the catch

quote.text: Uttar Pradesh is the size of France, Germany, Italy and Spain com­bined. Right, it is that big.

box.title: The book behind the argument
box.text: *In Service of the Republic*, by Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah, ar­gues that de­vel­op­ment is about dis­pers­ing power: co-equal ex­ec­u­tive, leg­isla­tive and ju­di­cial branches that check each other. India’s fail­ures, it says, come from an over­bear­ing, con­cen­trated Union. {047-R23}

sections.label: The problem
sections.head: Liberia here, Argentina there
sections.caption: India’s continental gaps
body: Start with het­ero­gene­ity, Ajay Shah said. Across India’s 3.3 mil­lion square kilo­me­tres, cul­tures and food habits dif­fer, as ev­ery­one knows. The eco­nom­ics dif­fers just as much.

CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey di­vides India into about a hun­dred ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions of roughly seven dis­tricts each. Average in­come in the rich­est is about five times that in the poor­est. {047-R02} Mobile phone own­er­ship among young women runs from 90 or 95 per cent in the best places to 5, 10 or 15 per cent in the worst.
The econ­o­mist Lant Pritchett once told Shah that India’s rich­est place di­vided by its poor­est gives the kind of ratio you get from Latin America’s rich­est place and Africa’s poor­est. {047-C02}
## Country-sized states

Amit Varma brought fig­ures from Nilakantan RS. Kerala’s life ex­pectancy is 75, like Argentina and Thailand; Uttar Pradesh’s is 64, what you would ex­pect from Liberia, Ethiopia and Haiti. {#lifeexp} Kerala’s in­fant mor­tal­ity, seven per thou­sand, is close to the USA’s six. Madhya Pradesh’s is 48.

From Karthik Muralidharan, Varma learnt that India’s 15 big­gest states would all rank among the world’s top 42 coun­tries by pop­u­la­tion. Uttar Pradesh alone, by his own sum, is France, Germany, Italy and Spain com­bined. {047-S02}

~ The av­er­age dis­trict, Muralidharan points out, is big­ger than 85 coun­tries. Those coun­tries would de­mand democ­racy, Varma said; an Indian dis­trict, with ev­ery­thing so cen­tralised, can­not have it.

quote.text: Uttar Pradesh is the size of France, Germany, Italy and Spain com­bined. Right, it is that big.

sections.label: The state’s job
sections.head: One size fits nobody
sections.caption: mosquitoes and civil service pay
body: Heterogeneity changes two ques­tions, Ajay Shah said: what the state should do, and how it should do it. North India may worry most about air qual­ity, Kerala about Arabian Sea cy­clones tear­ing at its coast­line.

Amit Varma’s clear­est ex­am­ple: Kerala has a prob­lem of di­a­betes and obe­sity, the heart­land one of mal­nu­tri­tion and stunt­ing. Send both the same cen­tral pol­icy, he said, and “peo­ple in Kerala are like WTF, this is not our prob­lem.” {047-C03}

The how varies too. Shah called it “a mad idea” that all civil ser­vants in India are paid es­sen­tially the same. In the rich parts, he said, they are paid a lit­tle too lit­tle; in the poor parts, too much. {047-C04}
## The mos­quito ques­tion

Shah’s favourite pub­lic-health ob­ses­sion is mos­qui­toes. Indians have given up on them, he said, but they can be con­trolled. {047-C05} Their char­ac­ter­is­tics change every 100 or 200 kilo­me­tres, shaped by local weather and the be­hav­iour of their vic­tims, so con­trol pro­grammes must vary by neigh­bour­hood. Maybe Ladakh has no mos­qui­toes at all.
Varma heard an album title: “Mosquitoes and Ladakh”, heavy metal, in fact. {047-J02}
~ He added a fig­ure from Karthik Muralidharan’s book: just 3 per cent of India’s bud­get is spent at the local level, against 50 per cent in China.

quote.text: It comes as a sur­prise to most peo­ple in India that ac­tu­ally mos­qui­toes can be con­trolled

sections.label: The principle
sections.head: Start at the bottom
sections.caption: the subsidiarity principle
body: The sub­sidiar­ity prin­ci­ple, Ajay Shah said, is a sim­ple de­sign rule: try to do each job of gov­ern­ment at the low­est pos­si­ble level, and go higher only when that fails. {047-C06} Can a vil­lage do mos­quito con­trol? Then the vil­lage should.

The European Union ap­plies it ques­tion by ques­tion: a com­mon cur­rency through the European Central Bank, de­fence through NATO, while per­sonal law re­flects Catholic think­ing in Portugal and Spain and more sec­u­lar norms in the north. Its les­son, Shah said: “Don’t draw lines on maps.” {047-C07}
## Villages and cities

Amit Varma raised B.R. Ambedkar’s ver­dict on the vil­lage as “a sink of lo­cal­ism, a den of ig­no­rance and nar­row mind­ed­ness”, the basis of his case for cen­tral­is­ing power. And what are states for? Since T20 ar­rived, Varma said, “states are kinda like ODIs.” {047-J06}

Shah is scep­ti­cal of vil­lages. One of about 150 house­holds, or 600 peo­ple, lacks the scale for enough civil ser­vants, politi­cians, com­pe­ti­tion and checks and bal­ances, and re­search finds the gains from vil­lage de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion weak. {047-C09}
~ Cities are an­other mat­ter: Bombay, with a lit­tle of New Bombay, has more peo­ple than Australia. Treating the 73rd and 74th Amendments as twins, Shah said, is one rea­son things have not worked.

quote.text: So I’m not a ro­man­tic about vil­lage level gov­ern­ment.

sections.label: The Indian way
sections.head: Delhi’s 65 per cent solution
sections.caption: the concurrent list and GST
body: India’s Constitution sorts the sub­jects of gov­ern­ment into a Union list, a state list and a con­cur­rent list. The con­cur­rent list, Ajay Shah said, “is a fan­tasy”: its framers pic­tured a wise chief min­is­ter of Maharashtra find­ing a mid­dle road with Jawaharlal Nehru. {#fantasy}

In the fine print, once the Union leg­is­lates on a con­cur­rent sub­ject, it wins. Planners then eyed the state list, through cen­trally spon­sored schemes: run ed­u­ca­tion the Union’s way and it pays 65 per cent, hi­jack­ing the state’s 35. {#sixtyfive}
Much of the Constitution, Shah ob­served, would be flagged by a pla­gia­rism test as com­ing from the Government of India Act of 1935. {047-J10}
## Money for cities
The 73rd and 74th Amendments, pushed under Rajiv Gandhi, did not go far enough, Shah said. State fi­nance com­mis­sions are often never set up, and lack data and neu­tral­ity when they are.

GST changes that, be­cause each sale can be traced to a shop and so to a city. Shah’s num­bers: a sin­gle rate of about 10 per cent, with roughly three to the Union, two to the state and five to the city. {047-C10}

~ Amit Varma re­called Shruti Rajagopalan’s talk on how Nehru amended the Constitution when­ever he wanted to do some­thing un­con­sti­tu­tional. {047-S09} A car­toon had the par­lia­ment book­shop ex­plain that it did not stock pe­ri­od­i­cals.

quote.text: I think there should be no cen­trally spon­sored schemes. And I think the union should va­cate the con­cur­rent list.

sections.label: The heresy
sections.head: Exit, voice and Bangalore
sections.caption: migration as exit
body: Amit Varma said there were two Ajay Shahs: a sober man of his­tory, and a heretic whose mad ideas make sense. He de­manded that the heretic present him­self. {047-J11}

The heretic began with mi­gra­tion. In American fed­er­al­ism, Shah said, peo­ple who dis­like their city or state move: the “exit” of Albert O Hirschman’s *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty*. Indians are used to loy­alty or a lit­tle voice. {047-R16}
From James C. Scott he took the in­sight that early states com­peted not for land but for peo­ple. When a gov­ern­ment works badly, he said, the peo­ple will leave. {047-R17}
## Against a lux­ury be­lief

Shah called the lament for mi­grants who left a vil­lage par­adise for a city slum a lux­ury be­lief of the rich in air-conditioned rooms. Across North India, he said, an am­bi­tious young engineer’s dream is to go to Amdavad, Bombay, Pune, Hyderabad, Bangalore or Madras. {047-C11}

Varma’s caveat: Indian states feel this com­pe­ti­tion only weakly, be­cause only a tiny chunk of tax money comes to them. Shah’s an­swers were a GST slice for states and cities, and the ob­ser­va­tion that mi­gra­tion off­sets fall­ing birth rates in pros­per­ous states.
~ A bee, mean­while, kept cir­cling Varma. “It seems to have fallen in love with me,” he said. {047-J12}

quote.text: And I re­joice and ap­plaud the guts of the peo­ple who mi­grate.

portraits.caption: James C. Scott
portraits.credit: SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0

sections.label: The catch
sections.head: The dictator next door
sections.caption: chief ministers and a hundred states
body: Decentralisation has a catch, Ajay Shah warned. A chief min­is­ter in India, he said, is a lit­tle bit of a dic­ta­tor. Legislatures pro­vide lit­tle check, noth­ing like the Rajya Sabha forces ne­go­ti­a­tion, and state ju­di­cia­ries are often cowed. {047-C13}

The same logic runs through *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar: de­vel­op­ment is about dis­pers­ing power among co-equal branches that check each other, and states and cities need that as much as the Union. {047-C14}

Some ad­vo­cates of hand­ing power to the states, Shah said, seem quite com­fort­able with a chief min­is­ter as dic­ta­tor. Amit Varma took the point as a warn­ing against shal­low think­ing: de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion taken up as a mantra rather than rea­soned from first prin­ci­ples.
## The way out

Shah’s fixes in­clude a GST slice for cities, sep­a­rate think­ing for cities and vil­lages, po­lit­i­cal re­form in states and cities, and an in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity for every gov­ern­ment. Strip out the knowl­edge, he said, and gov­ern­ment be­comes a raw power project. {047-C16}
His thumb rule is about a hun­dred states, many of them cities. {047-C15} West Bengal could be two or three, one of them Calcutta, deal­ing di­rectly with the Finance Commission.
~ That fits the present Constitution, Shah said, which mat­ters when draft­ing skills are poor and amend­ments are fraught with dif­fi­culty.

quote.text: If you get the checks and bal­ances, if you get a sen­si­ble re­pub­lic, then the eco­nomic growth will in­evitably fol­low.

Every state re­quires a com­men­su­rate in­tel­lec­tual com­mu­nity. You need the data sets, the thinkers, the re­search pa­pers, the pub­lic de­bate, the crit­i­cism. Without that no gov­ern­ment ever works well.

p3.title: Stories from the ground
p3.deck: A dog, two cats, a Dutch tank battalion and the mayors who became ministers

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a dog bite, a government clinic and Kerala
stories.head: A bite, and no needless needles
body: Susan Thomas was bit­ten by the fam­ily dog. She al­ways apol­o­gises that it was her fault, Ajay Shah said: she was trou­bling the dog. Susan, he ex­plained, has very high stan­dards for good be­hav­iour.
What fol­lowed, in Kerala, was a list of sur­prises. Amit Varma sug­gested they began with the bit­ing.

Surprise num­ber one: the fam­ily took her to a gov­ern­ment clinic. In most of India, Shah said, peo­ple like them would go to a pri­vate es­tab­lish­ment. In Kerala there was no fric­tion; it was the ob­vi­ous thing to do.
Surprise num­ber two: the doc­tor was there. The fa­cil­ity was not va­cant, and he was smart, com­pe­tent and sen­si­ble.
He asked the cor­rect ques­tions. Is it a fam­ily dog? Is the dog at home and fine? Will it be under ob­ser­va­tion? Then he gave her a lit­tle an­ti­sep­tic and sent her home. {#antiseptic}

If the dog had ra­bies, Shah ex­plained, it would col­lapse and go crazy first, and that would be the time to start vac­ci­nat­ing the human. Most doc­tors in India, pri­vate or pub­lic, would in­stead “blast” a course of ra­bies vac­ci­na­tion.
In most states, he said, the fam­ily would not think of a gov­ern­ment fa­cil­ity, which would most likely be va­cant, or staffed by “a low qual­ity hack” who would blast nine in­jec­tions.
~ The moral, for Shah, was India’s im­mense di­ver­sity. “I may be rad­i­cal in my views on the health sys­tem,” he said, “but I re­spect what Kerala has in a gov­ern­ment run health sys­tem.”
stories.why: Policy can­not be one size fits all, Shah ar­gued, when state ca­pac­ity it­self varies so much. Radical re­form for most of India’s gov­ern­ment health sys­tem should still leave alone what Kerala has built. {047-S04}
stories.postscript: Amit Varma’s own doc­tor, Lancelot Pinto, saw him through COVID twice on parac­eta­mol and cough syrup. {047-S05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Susan Thomas and the dog bite

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells Pranay Kotasthane’s fable
stories.head: Split the bread, keep the bread
body: Two cats find a piece of bread under a table at the same mo­ment and fight over it. A canny old mon­key in a tree of­fers to me­di­ate and make equal pieces.

He breaks the bread, but one half is big­ger, so he eats a bit of it. Too much: now the other half is big­ger. He keeps going until two tiny equal bits re­main, then takes those too, as pay­ment for his labour. {047-S08}

Amit Varma had the fable from a news­let­ter post by Pranay Kotasthane. {047-R12} Its point: Indian states fight over hor­i­zon­tal de­vo­lu­tion, which state gets what share, and talk too lit­tle about ver­ti­cal de­vo­lu­tion, how much reaches the states at all.
~ The South com­plains that it con­trib­utes more than the North, Varma said, while the cen­tre gives only 42 per cent to the states.
stories.why: While the states quar­rel over their shares, the big­ger ques­tion goes unasked: how much of the bread the cen­tre keeps. For real de­cen­tral­i­sa­tion, on Kotasthane’s ar­gu­ment, the ver­ti­cal split mat­ters more than the hor­i­zon­tal one.
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah noted that the episode now had “a dog, a cat, a mon­key”. Varma added: “And tanks, many, many tanks.” {047-J08}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the monkey and the two cats

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah, unable to resist, on the Dutch army
stories.head: Dutch money, German command
body: Ajay Shah said he could not re­sist talk­ing about tanks. Amit Varma sighed: “You can never re­sist talk­ing about tanks.” {047-J03}
After the Second World War, Shah said, the Netherlands de­cided to let it go that Germany had in­vaded it a cou­ple of times, and went back to buy­ing German tanks. {047-J04}

But a small NATO mem­ber with per­haps twenty tanks found that run­ning its own lo­gis­tics tail and main­te­nance was silly at that scale. So it told the Germans: “We’ll pay for the tanks, but the tanks will be con­trolled by the German army on our be­half.” Dutch sol­diers served in units fully in­te­grated into the German army. {047-S07}
~ Arrangements like this, Shah said, have taken place all over Europe.
stories.why: Instead of defin­ing the state by lines on maps, Shah ar­gued, de­cide each func­tion at the scale where it works: one cur­rency, shared de­fence, pooled tanks and local per­sonal law. {047-C07}
stories.postscript: Varma pic­tured a thumb­nail of Shah peer­ing out of a tank, and ended the episode: “Ajay in a tank.”

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Dutch tanks

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the freedom movement’s apprenticeship
stories.head: Salem first, then the nation
body: Not so long ago, Amit Varma said, India had em­pow­ered may­ors. C. Rajagopalachari was ef­fec­tively mayor of Salem in 1917, as chair­man of the mu­nic­i­pal board. {#salem} Jawaharlal Nehru held a sim­i­lar po­si­tion in Allahabad in 1923.
Chittaranjan Das held it in Calcutta, and then Subhas Chandra Bose. Sardar Patel, Varma said, was prom­i­nent in the Allahabad mu­nic­i­pal coun­cil.

Under the British, local gov­ern­ments were em­pow­ered to do local tasks that the colo­nial gov­ern­ment could not be both­ered with, and they trained fu­ture lead­ers. Those who be­came prime min­is­ter and home min­is­ter, Varma said, did not sim­ply go from ac­tivists to politi­cians. “They knew gov­er­nance, they cared deeply about it, they un­der­stood pub­lic fi­nance.” {047-S01}
~ After in­de­pen­dence, he said, India kept most of the colo­nial co­er­cive su­per­struc­ture and lost that lit­tle part of the puz­zle.
stories.why: Running cities was where the free­dom movement’s lead­ers learnt gov­er­nance and pub­lic fi­nance. In los­ing em­pow­ered local gov­ern­ment, Varma sug­gested, India lost the cru­cible out of which its first prime min­is­ter and home min­is­ter emerged.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the freedom fighters as city bosses

overheard.text: I have names for the three states. Calcutta, West and Bengal.
overheard.who: Amit Varma, as Ajay Shah proposed splitting West Bengal

quiz.q: Which four European countries, combined, match Uttar Pradesh’s population by Amit Varma’s own calculation?
quiz.a: France, Germany, Italy and Spain, all run by a sin­gle state gov­ern­ment.

quiz.q: What does the subsidiarity principle say, and which institution did Ajay Shah trace it to?
quiz.a: Place each func­tion at the low­est work­able level; the Catholic Church prac­tised it for cen­turies.

quiz.q: Why did the Kerala doctor give Susan Thomas only antiseptic after the dog bite?
quiz.a: A rabid dog would col­lapse first; that would be the time to vac­ci­nate.

quiz.q: In Pranay Kotasthane’s fable, what does the monkey finally take as payment for his labour?
quiz.a: The last two tiny, equal bits of bread, after eat­ing the rest him­self.

quiz.q: How would Ajay Shah split a single-rate GST of about 10 per cent?
quiz.a: Roughly three per cent to the Union, two to the state, five to the city.

quiz.q: Between Test cricket and T20, what did Amit Varma say states were like?
quiz.a: ODIs, the mid­dle for­mat that peo­ple said was no longer needed.

glossary.def: Placing each gov­ern­ment func­tion at the low­est level that can han­dle it.
Subjects both Union and states may leg­is­late on; the Union pre­vails.
A Union pro­gramme on a state sub­ject, part-paid if run Delhi’s way.
How much of the tax pool the cen­tre passes down to states.
A com­fort­able person’s lament, here for mi­grants who leave their vil­lages.
Indian slang for a basic prin­ci­ple, as in Pinto’s don’t-overmedicate ap­proach.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 47. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); St. Peter’s Basilica (Alvesgaspar, CC BY-SA 4.0); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Albert O. Hirschman (Sgt. Charles James, public domain); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Jane Jacobs (Phil Stanziola, public domain).

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: CMIE Consumer Pyramids dx
shelf.creator: CMIE
shelf.why: CMIE’s house­hold sur­vey (about 190,000 house­holds, three times a year, across some 100 ho­mo­ge­neous re­gions) makes India’s di­ver­sity mea­sur­able, from five­fold in­come gaps be­tween re­gions to how many house­holds re­ally live off farm­ing.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
shelf.why: Three schol­ars in­vent un­con­ven­tional, in­tu­itive mea­sures of women’s em­pow­er­ment, from who or­ders the gro­ceries to women in pris­ons and solo travel, along­side Amit’s own: ris­ing di­vorce rates.

shelf.title: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s provoca­tive ar­gu­ment that ris­ing di­vorce rates, often lamented as ‘be­com­ing like the West’, show more women gain­ing the agency and means to leave bad mar­riages.

shelf.title: South vs North
shelf.creator: Nilakantan RS
shelf.why: It sup­plies strik­ing com­par­isons: life ex­pectancy of 75 in Kerala ver­sus 64 in UP, and in­fant mor­tal­ity of 7 in Kerala ver­sus 48 in Madhya Pradesh.

shelf.title: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Nilakantan RS
shelf.why: RS Nilakantan on how dif­fer­ently South India’s needs look from the North’s, though the North’s pri­or­i­ties drive na­tional pol­icy, and on the North-South dis­par­i­ties be­hind that.

shelf.title: Accelerating India’s Development
shelf.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: Karthik Muralidharan’s book is the source of strik­ing facts the hosts use: the av­er­age dis­trict is big­ger than 85 coun­tries, only 3% of India’s bud­get is spent lo­cally against 50% in China, and more spend­ing on build­ings, school bags or ‘better’ teach­ers does noth­ing for learn­ing out­comes.

shelf.title: Karthik Muralidharan Examines the Indian State (Episode 290) and Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat’s Burden (Episode 375) of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: These are where Amit first learned that India’s 15 big­gest states would each rank among the world’s top 42 coun­tries by pop­u­la­tion, and where they dis­cuss India’s tiny local-level spend­ing.

shelf.title: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
shelf.why: Dr Lancelot Pinto, one of the rare doc­tors who reads pa­pers daily, on med­i­cal prac­tice and how overtreat­ment driven by pa­tient de­mand cost lives dur­ing COVID.

shelf.title: Brave New World
shelf.creator: Vasant Dhar
shelf.why: Vasant Dhar’s pod­cast, which Amit calls great and backs as the show of a very dear friend.

shelf.title: The Fable of the Monkey and the Two Cats
shelf.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
shelf.why: Amit calls it a ‘great news­let­ter post’.

shelf.title: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 17 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
shelf.why: Pranay Kotasthane on how schemes de­signed in Delhi fail to fit the very dif­fer­ent needs of India’s states and work as a back­door for cen­tral con­trol over state sub­jects.

shelf.title: Shruti Rajagopalan on India’s many constitutional amendments
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s talk trac­ing how India’s Constitution has been amended from Nehru on­wards when­ever gov­ern­ments wanted to do some­thing un­con­sti­tu­tional, until amend­ment be­came the rou­tine way to make the un­con­sti­tu­tional con­sti­tu­tional.

shelf.title: Urban Governance in India (Episode 31 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shruti ex­plains why city gov­er­nance is bad: power and ac­count­abil­ity are not linked.

shelf.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
shelf.creator: Albert O Hirschman
shelf.why: Hirschman’s frame­work of exit, voice and loy­alty shows what India un­der­uses: Indians rely on loy­alty or a lit­tle voice, while Americans exit, mov­ing if they dis­like their city or state.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: The Power Broker
shelf.creator: Robert Caro
shelf.why: Caro’s mas­ter­piece works on three lev­els: a bi­og­ra­phy of Robert Moses, a bi­og­ra­phy of New York re­shaped by top-down plan­ning, and a study of how power cor­rupts an ide­al­is­tic man.

shelf.title: Triumph of the City
shelf.creator: Edward Glaeser
shelf.why: Glaeser ex­plains that cities are great be­cause they pack clever peo­ple close to­gether, while ad­mit­ting dense cities can be ter­ri­ble (crime, slums, pub­lic health), which makes good gov­er­nance the real chal­lenge.

shelf.title: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
shelf.creator: Jane Jacobs
shelf.why: Jane Jacobs’s ar­gu­ment that cities are about peo­ple, not build­ings and high­ways, and grow or­gan­i­cally from the bot­tom up: spon­ta­neous order and metis against Robert Moses’s high mod­ernism.

shelf.title: Bimal Patel’s forthcoming book
shelf.creator: Bimal Patel
shelf.why: Patel is India’s pre-eminent urban thinker and un­der­stands town plan­ning like al­most no­body else in India.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

laughs.text: After Ajay’s mos­quito ob­ses­sion and his line about there per­haps being no mos­qui­toes in Ladakh, Amit says: “Mosquitoes and Ladakh would be an in­cred­i­ble title for a rock album, a heavy metal album in fact.”

The tank run­ning gag. When Ajay says he can’t re­sist bring­ing some­thing up, Amit groans, “You can never re­sist talk­ing about tanks. Fine, Ajay Shah, one more time let’s talk about tanks.” He then pic­tures a thumb­nail of Ajay peer­ing out of a tank and signs off the episode with “Ajay in a tank.”

Ajay voices the Dutch at­ti­tude to Germany after WWII: “Okay, fine, we for­give you, you know, we know you in­vaded us a cou­ple of times, but we let it go”, and then they went back to buy­ing German tanks.

Amit retells a joke from Vasant Dhar. Vasant’s friend Bubba claims to know ev­ery­one. At Trump Tower the sec­re­tary says Donald will be so happy to see him. At the White House, Biden spots him, rushes out, and falls over a cou­ple of times on the way. At the Vatican, Vasant loses Bubba in the crowd, and then the Pope ap­pears on the bal­cony with Bubba be­side him. The man next to Vasant taps him and asks: “Excuse me, who’s that guy with Bubba?”

Amit on the awk­ward mid­dle tier of gov­ern­ment: “When T20 cricket be­came pop­u­lar, peo­ple said Test cricket ra­hega, T20 ra­hega, we don’t need ODIs any­more. So I think states are kinda like ODIs.”

Amit: the pop­u­la­tion of Iceland equals that of Mumbai’s Versova. Ajay: about 300,000, “and half of them are fish­er­men.” Amit: “Iceland or Versova?” Ajay: “Iceland.” Amit: “But yeah, we have fish­er­men too and we are proud of them.”
As an­i­mals pile up in the episode, Ajay says, “In this episode we’ve got a dog, a cat, a mon­key.” Amit adds: “And tanks, many, many tanks.”

Amit, dead­pan, after Ajay held up his phone while say­ing ‘mo­bile phone’: “I must thank you from the bot­tom of my heart for as­sum­ing that I am as stupid as I am... now I know and I feel so good that I have gained new knowl­edge today and I know what a mo­bile phone looks like.”

Ajay on how much of India’s Constitution was car­ried over from colo­nial law: “It is re­mark­able how much pla­gia­rism test would pick up things in the con­sti­tu­tion of India that come from the Government of India Act.”
Amit says there are two Ajay Shahs: a sober, an­a­lyt­i­cal man of his­tory, and “a heretic who thinks mad ideas and all of those mad ideas make sense.” He de­mands that the heretic present him­self.

A bee keeps cir­cling Amit’s head: “It seems to have fallen in love with me, and while my charms are un­doubted, I would not wel­come this par­tic­u­lar at­ten­tion.” Ajay links it to the song lyric be­hind the title of the show’s first episode, and Amit sup­plies the line: “Dragonflies are busy buzzing me.”
Amit on Ajay’s odd verb choices: “I love the way you com­bine un­ex­pected verbs and nouns, like in a pre­vi­ous episode you said solv­ing a moun­tain. And over here you’re like build­ing a book.”
Ajay opens the show with a riff on Julius Caesar’s ‘lean and hun­gry look’: “Your Amit has a hun­gry look. Such men are dan­ger­ous. Amit, what dan­ger­ous ideas do you have to offer us?”

Amit quotes B.R. Ambedkar’s fa­mous ver­dict, “What is a vil­lage but a sink of lo­cal­ism, a den of ig­no­rance and nar­row mind­ed­ness”. He calls it Ambedkar’s ar­gu­ment for cen­tral­is­ing power, given caste and the treat­ment of women in vil­lages. It raises the real puz­zle of how far local gov­ern­ment should go.
